summary: Describes methods for encapsulating layer 2 protocol data units such as Frame Relay, ATM, or Ethernet for transport across an MPLS network. It documents the so-called draft-martini protocol, which has since been superseded by pseudowire specifications such as RFC 4447. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Different network types can be wrapped up and sent across a shared network. This note describes one old wrapping method, since replaced by newer ones.

questions: how to carry layer 2 frames over mpls
how to carry frame relay over mpls
subtitle: Wrapping layer 2 networks inside an MPLS tunnel.

tldr.problem: Different layer 2 protocols (Frame Relay, ATM, Ethernet, PPP, HDLC) need to be transported across MPLS networks while preserving their operation and handling packet sequencing and loss.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4905 specifies how to encapsulate layer 2 PDUs with a control word containing a sequence number, flags, and length field, allowing each protocol to be tunneled transparently across an MPLS backbone.
tldr.outcome: Operators could use a shared MPLS network to carry multiple layer 2 protocols from different customers, though this specification has been superseded by the Pseudowire Emulation (PWE3) RFCs.

facts.label: Layer 2 protocols supported
facts.value: Frame Relay, ATM, Ethernet, HDLC, PPP

today: RFC 4905 is Historic and superseded by the Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3) specifications, particularly RFC 4447 and related RFCs such as RFC 4717 (ATM), RFC 4618 (PPP/HDLC), and RFC 4448 (Ethernet). This RFC documents the draft-martini protocol used in deployed implementations and MUST NOT be used for new implementations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4905 describes the so-called draft-martini protocol for carrying layer 2 protocol data units (PDUs) across MPLS networks. An emulated virtual circuit (VC) transports layer 2 traffic from an ingress router to an egress router, preserving the protocol as if the MPLS network were transparent. Multiple emulated VCs can be multiplexed in a single MPLS tunnel, each identified by an MPLS label.

The document specifies encapsulation for six layer 2 protocols: Frame Relay, ATM (both AAL5 and cell modes), Ethernet with VLAN, plain Ethernet, HDLC, and PPP. This protocol has been superseded by PWE3 (RFC 4447) and related RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: Different network types can all run inside MPLS. This spec says how to wrap Frame Relay, ATM, Ethernet, and other protocols so they work when tunneled through an MPLS network.

sections.title: Control Word and Encapsulation
sections.content:
The core of the encapsulation is a 4-byte control word that precedes each layer 2 PDU. The control word contains:

  • Reserved bits (4): Set to 0.
  • Flags (4): Protocol-specific flags such as BECN/FECN for Frame Relay or EFCI/CLP for ATM.
  • Length (6 bits): If the packet (including control word and payload) is under 64 bytes, this holds the length; otherwise 0. This allows removal of padding at the egress.
  • Sequence number (16 bits): Increments from 1 for each packet on a VC. A value of 0 means no sequencing. The egress can detect out-of-order or lost packets.

At the ingress, the layer 2 header is stripped, the control word is added, and the MPLS label is prepended. At the egress, the reverse happens: the label is removed, the control word is inspected, and the layer 2 header is regenerated.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet gets a header saying what is inside it, how long it is, and what number it is. That way the far end knows if a packet got lost or came in the wrong order.

sections.title: Protocol-Specific Handling
sections.content:
Frame Relay: The control word flags carry the BECN, FECN, DE, and C/R bits from the Frame Relay header. The egress regenerates the Frame Relay frame.

ATM AAL5 mode: Multiple ATM cells are reassembled at the ingress into an AAL5 CPCS-SDU, then transported as a single packet with the EFCI and CLP bits carried in the control word.

ATM cell mode: Individual ATM cells are transported with their VPI, VCI, PTI, and CLP fields carried transparently. Multiple cells fit in one frame.

Ethernet and VLAN: The entire frame (minus preamble and FCS) is transported. The control word is optional for Ethernet.

HDLC and PPP: These are transported with the control word optional, preserving protocol and payload but stripping media-specific framing.
sections.plainLanguage: Different protocols put different information in the control word. For Frame Relay it is congestion bits, for ATM it is priority bits. For Ethernet there is often no control word at all.

sections.title: Sequencing and Out-of-Order Handling
sections.content:
The sequence number in the control word starts at 1 and increments by 1 for each packet on a VC. When it reaches 65535 it wraps to 1. The egress router checks the sequence number to detect loss and out-of-order delivery.

If a packet arrives out of order, the egress can either drop it or reorder it, depending on the implementation. If sequencing is not supported by the ingress, the sequence number field is set to 0 and the egress ignores it.

The MTU must be large enough to encapsulate the largest layer 2 PDU plus headers (typically 12+ bytes more than the largest PDU). If a PDU exceeds the tunnel MTU or the egress MTU, it is dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet is numbered so the far end can tell if any are missing or out of order. Big packets that do not fit are dropped.
